newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Yilmaz faces task of restoring stability.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Yilmaz faces task of restoring stability.

text.p: Turkey's new Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz faces the daunting task of restoring stability to a country racked by months of political chaos and keeping Islamists out of power.
But Yilmaz's secularist coalition must still win a confidence vote, expected to be held on July 12, and the anti-Islamist forces in parliament have already shown signs of disunity.
Conservative Yilmaz was on Tuesday to press on with shaping a government programme among members of his uneasy secularist alliance, set up to keep the embattled Islamists out of power.

Ahead of his government's first cabinet meeting on Monday, Yilmaz said his left-right coalition would end disputes about the role of Islam in public life and possible intervention by the restive military in secular, NATO member Turkey.
"It will be a government that raises the profile of civilian, democratic and freedom-loving values," Yilmaz told reporters after his appointment by President Suleyman Demirel.
Yilmaz replaced Necmettin Erbakan, who resigned two weeks ago after a row with the army over religious activism that precipitated the end of his year as Turkey's first Islamist leader.
The stock market, which rose over 10 percent last week on hopes for a Yilmaz-led coalition, welcomed the news of his appointment. The main Istanbul index closed 2.31 percent higher on Monday.

Yilmaz will face intense pressure from the business community to address Turkey's chronic economic woes of high inflation and ballooning deficits which, economists say, Erbakan's year in power did little to alleviate.

Discord has already emerged among secularists whose support is vital to the success of Yilmaz's government. The Republican People's Party (CHP) said the backing it has promised him should not be taken for granted.

"If this government thinks the CHP cannot withdraw support, and if it acts against the CHP...I am saying today that the CHP reaction will be very strong," senior party member Ali Topuz told a news conference.
The party has said its 49 MPs will back Yilmaz at the confidence vote but it disagrees with him over the date of early elections.
Yilmaz, a staid conservative, said he would debate a date for possible early polls with coalition members, in an apparent backtrack from a previous commitment to elections in early 1998.

The coalition's chances of surviving a confidence vote in parliament have been boosted by a wave of defections from a rival conservative party. Yilmaz now has around 12 more MPs on paper than his opponents in the 550-member national assembly.

The coalition protocol, distributed on Monday, said the government would maintain the country's campaign against a Kurdish rebel insurgency in the southeast of the country which has claimed 26,000 lives since 1984.
